content.title: Countable and uncountable nouns and quantifiers
content.instructions: Complete each sentence. Where options are given, choose the correct one; otherwise write ONE word. Before you answer, decide whether the noun is countable or uncountable.

items.prompt: The number of students who own a laptop has increased, while the ___ of time they spend reading printed books has fallen.
items.model_answer: The number of students who own a laptop has increased, while the amount of time they spend reading printed books has fallen.
items.explanation: 'Time' is uncountable here, so use 'the amount of'. 'The number of' is only for plural countable nouns (the number of students).

items.prompt: In 2020, ___ people travelled by air than in 2019 because of the pandemic.
items.model_answer: In 2020, fewer people travelled by air than in 2019 because of the pandemic.
items.explanation: 'People' is a plural countable noun, so the comparative is 'fewer'. 'Less' goes with uncountable nouns (less traffic, less money). Examiners notice this error in Task 1 comparisons.

items.prompt: Recent ___ suggests that bilingual children perform better at certain problem-solving tasks.
items.model_answer: Recent research suggests that bilingual children perform better at certain problem-solving tasks.
items.explanation: 'Research' is uncountable in academic English: no plural -s and no 'a'. To count it, use 'a study / studies' or 'a piece of research'. The verb is singular ('suggests').

items.prompt: Tourists can find a great deal of useful ___ about local attractions online.
items.model_answer: Tourists can find a great deal of useful information about local attractions online.
items.explanation: 'Information' is always uncountable: no -s and no 'an'. It combines with 'a great deal of', 'much' and 'a piece of'. 'Advice', 'knowledge' and 'equipment' behave in the same way.

items.prompt: I think there's far too ___ traffic in my city centre, especially during the rush hour.
items.model_answer: I think there's far too much traffic in my city centre, especially during the rush hour.
items.explanation: 'Traffic' is uncountable, so use 'too much', not 'too many'. In Speaking, 'far too much' adds natural emphasis.

items.prompt: Only a small ___ of respondents said they were satisfied with the service.
items.model_answer: Only a small number of respondents said they were satisfied with the service.
items.explanation: 'Respondents' is a plural countable noun, so 'a small number of' is correct; 'proportion', 'percentage' and 'minority' also suit survey data. 'A small amount of respondents' is wrong because 'amount' is used with uncountable nouns.

items.prompt: Many rural schools lack modern laboratory ___, so science lessons are mostly theoretical.
items.model_answer: Many rural schools lack modern laboratory equipment, so science lessons are mostly theoretical.
items.explanation: 'Equipment' is uncountable and has no plural form. To count items, say 'pieces of equipment' or name them (microscopes, computers).

items.prompt: Air pollution fell in ___ of the three cities; in fact, all three recorded an increase.
items.model_answer: Air pollution fell in none of the three cities; in fact, all three recorded an increase.
items.explanation: 'None of' + plural noun means 'zero out of three or more'. For exactly two items, use 'neither of'. The second clause ('all three recorded an increase') shows that the meaning is zero.

items.prompt: Investment in wind power rose sharply in ___ Denmark and Germany, although Denmark started earlier.
items.model_answer: Investment in wind power rose sharply in both Denmark and Germany, although Denmark started earlier.
items.explanation: 'Both … and …' refers to two items together. For two items with a negative meaning, use 'neither … nor …'; for more than two, use 'all (of)'.

items.prompt: There were very ___ jobs available in the region, so many young people moved to the capital.
items.model_answer: There were very few jobs available in the region, so many young people moved to the capital.
items.explanation: 'Jobs' is plural countable, so use '(very) few'. 'Little' is for uncountable nouns (very little work). Note that 'few' is negative in meaning ('not many'), whereas 'a few' means 'some'.
